This is a per-feature generalization of SDEdit. Where SDEdit renoises the whole image by one global amount, Equation ˜ 4 renoises each feature by its own amount 1 − τ 1-\tau .

High- τ \tau features start from the real source latent and receive near-zero transport, so they are preserved, while low- τ \tau features start mostly from the corruption and are painted into target content. In the τ → 1 \tau{\to}1 limit a feature is initialized at the source latent, keeping preserved regions strongly source-anchored rather than resampling them. The task-matched corruption ϵ α \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\alpha} in Equation ˜ 4 is not always isotropic. Only appearance (color, stain, texture) should move. There, isotropic ϵ \boldsymbol{\epsilon} needlessly destroys content in exactly the regions τ \tau frees, forcing the flow to hallucinate the geometry back. A high- τ \tau feature remains inactive through most of the trajectory, while a low- τ \tau feature becomes active earlier and translates sooner. A hard threshold would zero the gradient with respect to τ \tau and break this, whereas the sharpness T T trades gradient flow against gate crispness, with T → 0 T\!\to\!0 recovering a hard SDEdit-style cutover. The three roles are thus separated yet jointly optimized. The frozen flow supplies the base trajectory, the correction C ϕ C_{\phi} the deflecting velocity, and 𝒯 ψ \mathcal{T}_{\psi} learns per feature where and when it is applied. Either criterion alone can be misleading. A method may improve realism by altering excessive source content, whereas high source similarity may result from insufficient translation.
